stem: Which one of the following minerals is formed by decomposition of rocks, leaving a residual mass of weathered material?
solution:
**(b) Bauxite.**

Bauxite is formed by the decomposition of surface rocks and the removal of soluble constituents, which leaves a residual mass of weathered material containing the ore.

The other minerals occur in other modes:

- **Coal** is concentrated in beds or layers in sedimentary rocks.
- **Gold** occurs as a placer deposit in the sands of valley floors.
- **Zinc** is obtained from veins and lodes.
groundedIn: § Mode of Occurrence of Minerals — the third mode listed is decomposition of surface rocks and removal of soluble constituents, leaving a residual mass of weathered material containing ores, and the chapter says bauxite is formed this way; the same list places coal in sedimentary beds, gold in placer deposits and zinc among the metallic minerals obtained from veins and lodes

stem: Koderma, in Jharkhand is the leading producer of which one of the following minerals?
solution:
**(b) Mica.**

Mica deposits are found along the northern edge of the Chota Nagpur plateau, and the **Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand** is the leading producer.
groundedIn: § Non-Metallic Minerals — mica deposits are found in the northern edge of the Chota Nagpur plateau and the Koderma Gaya Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand is the leading producer

stem: Minerals are deposited and accumulated in the stratas of which of the following rocks?
solution:
**(a) Sedimentary rocks.**

In sedimentary rocks a number of minerals occur in **beds or layers**, formed as a result of deposition, accumulation and concentration in **horizontal strata**. Coal and some forms of iron ore were concentrated this way under long periods of great heat and pressure, while gypsum, potash salt and sodium salt were formed by evaporation.

In igneous and metamorphic rocks minerals occur instead in cracks, crevices, faults or joints, as veins and lodes.
groundedIn: § Mode of Occurrence of Minerals — in sedimentary rocks minerals occur in beds or layers formed by deposition, accumulation and concentration in horizontal strata, with coal and some forms of iron ore concentrated under great heat and pressure and gypsum, potash salt and sodium salt formed by evaporation

stem: Which one of the following minerals is contained in the Monazite sand?
solution:
**(c) Thorium.**

The **Monazite sands of Kerala** are rich in thorium. Thorium and uranium are used for generating atomic or nuclear power; uranium and thorium are also available in Jharkhand and in the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan.
groundedIn: § Nuclear or Atomic Energy — uranium and thorium available in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan are used for generating atomic power, and the Monazite sands of Kerala are also rich in thorium

context: Distinguish between the following in not more than 30 words.
stem: Distinguish between ferrous and non-ferrous minerals.
solution:
| Ferrous minerals | Non-ferrous minerals |
|---|---|
| Contain iron — iron ore and manganese. | Contain no iron — copper, bauxite, lead, zinc and gold. |
| Account for about three-fourths of the value of production of metallic minerals. | India's reserves and production are not very satisfactory. |
| Provide a strong base for metallurgical industries. | Used in metallurgical, engineering and electrical industries. |
groundedIn: § Ferrous Minerals — they account for about three-fourths of the total value of the production of metallic minerals and provide a strong base for metallurgical industries, the section covering iron ore and manganese; § Non-Ferrous Minerals — India's reserves and production are not very satisfactory, and these minerals include copper, bauxite, lead, zinc and gold and play a vital role in metallurgical, engineering and electrical industries

context: Distinguish between the following in not more than 30 words.
stem: Distinguish between conventional and non-conventional sources of energy.
solution:
| Conventional sources | Non-conventional sources |
|---|---|
| Firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (both hydel and thermal). | Solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and atomic energy. |
| Mostly exhaustible fossil fuels, in long use; firewood and dung cake meet over 70 per cent of rural household needs. | Renewable sources, promoted because fossil fuels are costly, uncertain in supply and cause serious environmental problems. |
groundedIn: § Energy Resources — energy resources are classified as conventional and non-conventional, conventional sources including firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity and non-conventional sources including solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and atomic energy, with more than 70 per cent of rural household energy met by firewood and dung cake; § Non-Conventional Sources of Energy — rising prices and potential shortages of oil and gas and the serious environmental problems of fossil fuels create a pressing need for renewable sources

context: Answer the following questions in about 30 words.
solution:
Geologists define a mineral as a **homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure**.

Minerals are found in varied forms in nature, ranging from the hardest diamond to the softest talc, and rocks are combinations of minerals.
groundedIn: § Study of Minerals by Geographers — the chapter's opening section, whose own sub-heading is set smaller than the body text and so is not itself citable, gives the geologists' definition of a mineral as a homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure, notes the range from the hardest diamond to the softest talc, and says rocks are combinations of homogenous substances called minerals

context: Answer the following questions in about 30 words.
stem: How are minerals formed in igneous and metamorphic rocks?
solution:
In igneous and metamorphic rocks minerals occur in the **cracks, crevices, faults or joints**. The smaller occurrences are called **veins** and the larger are called **lodes**.

They are formed when minerals in liquid, molten or gaseous form are forced upward through cavities towards the earth's surface, cooling and solidifying as they rise. Tin, copper, zinc and lead are obtained from such veins and lodes.
groundedIn: § Mode of Occurrence of Minerals — in igneous and metamorphic rocks minerals may occur in cracks, crevices, faults or joints, the smaller occurrences called veins and the larger lodes, formed when minerals in liquid, molten and gaseous forms are forced upward through cavities towards the surface and cool and solidify as they rise, yielding tin, copper, zinc and lead

context: Answer the following questions in about 30 words.
stem: Why do we need to conserve mineral resources?
solution:
1. Mineral resources are **finite and non-renewable** — the geological processes of mineral formation are so slow that the rate of replenishment is infinitely small compared with the present rate of consumption.
2. Workable mineral deposits are only about **one per cent of the earth's crust**.
3. Continued extraction raises costs, as ore comes from greater depths and its quality falls.
groundedIn: § Conservation of Minerals — the total volume of workable mineral deposits is one per cent of the earth's crust, the geological processes of mineral formation are so slow that rates of replenishment are infinitely small compared with present rates of consumption, mineral resources are therefore finite and non-renewable, and continued extraction of ores leads to increasing costs as extraction comes from greater depths along with decrease in quality

context: Answer the following questions in about 120 words.
stem: Describe the distribution of coal in India.
solution:
In India coal occurs in rock series of **two main geological ages**.

**1. Gondwana coal**, a little over 200 million years in age, holds the major resources of **metallurgical coal**. It is located in the **Damodar valley (West Bengal–Jharkhand)**, where **Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro** are the important coalfields. The **Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys** also contain coal deposits.

**2. Tertiary coal**, only about 55 million years old, occurs in the north-eastern states of **Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland**.

Coal also occurs in different forms according to the degree of compression and the depth and time of burial — **peat**, **lignite**, **bituminous** and **anthracite**. The principal **lignite** reserves are at **Neyveli in Tamil Nadu** and are used for the generation of electricity.

Since coal is a bulky material that loses weight on use, heavy industries and thermal power stations are located on or near the coalfields.
groundedIn: § Conventional Sources of Energy — coal occurs in rock series of two main geological ages, Gondwana a little over 200 million years old and tertiary about 55 million years old; the major Gondwana metallurgical coal resources are in the Damodar valley of West Bengal and Jharkhand with Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro as important coalfields, the Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys also carry deposits, tertiary coals occur in Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland, the principal lignite reserves are in Neyveli in Tamil Nadu, and coal being bulky the heavy industries and thermal power stations are located on or near the coalfields

context: Answer the following questions in about 120 words.
stem: Why do you think that solar energy has a bright future in India?
solution:
Solar energy has a bright future in India for the following reasons.

1. India is a **tropical country** blessed with an abundance of sunlight, so it has enormous possibilities of tapping solar energy.
2. **Photovoltaic technology** converts sunlight directly into electricity, so the resource can be used without a fuel supply.
3. Solar energy is **fast becoming popular in rural and remote areas**, and big solar power plants are being established in different parts of India.
4. These plants will **minimise the dependence of rural households on firewood and dung cakes**, which at present meet more than 70 per cent of rural energy requirements. That will contribute to **environmental conservation** and to an **adequate supply of manure** for agriculture.
5. Growing consumption has made the country increasingly dependent on coal, oil and gas, whose rising prices, potential shortages and serious environmental problems make renewable sources a pressing need.
groundedIn: § Solar Energy — India is a tropical country with enormous possibilities of tapping solar energy, photovoltaic technology converts sunlight directly into electricity, solar energy is fast becoming popular in rural and remote areas, and big solar power plants being established will minimise the dependence of rural households on firewood and dung cakes and so contribute to environmental conservation and adequate supply of manure in agriculture; § Non-Conventional Sources of Energy — India is blessed with an abundance of sunlight and has the largest programmes for developing renewable resources, while rising prices and potential shortages of oil and gas and the environmental problems of fossil fuels make renewables a pressing need; § Energy Resources — more than 70 per cent of rural household energy requirement is met by firewood and cattle dung cake
